opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there's a real gap today between how we build neural networks and how we reason about them. In PyTorch you write a model, you train it, you test it on some benchmarks, and you hope it behaves. But testing only ever covers the inputs you happened to try. What TorchLean is trying to do is bring the network itself into a setting like Lean, where you can state properties precisely and actually prove them, with the proof checked by the machine.

So there are a few layers of guarantees. The first is semantic: making sure the thing you're reasoning about is really the network you're running. A lot of verification work quietly assumes idealized math, real numbers, exact operations, while the actual model runs in floating point on a GPU. If your formal model and your executable model drift apart, your proof is about the wrong object. So a big part of the effort is having one definition of the network that you can both execute and reason about, and being honest about numerical semantics, including floating point and its error bounds.

The second layer is properties of the network itself: robustness, meaning if you perturb the input within some bound, the output doesn't change by more than some amount; Lipschitz bounds; monotonicity; or, for the scientific machine learning work I care about, like neural operators, physical constraints such as conservation laws or stability of a learned simulator over long rollouts. These are things you really want certified if a model goes into a weather forecast or an engineering design loop.

The third layer is about the verification tools themselves. There are great bound-propagation and verification algorithms out there, but they're large pieces of software, and they can have bugs. If the verifier is wrong, the certificate means nothing. In a proof assistant, you can have the verifier produce a certificate that a small, trusted kernel checks. So the trust moves from "I believe this big codebase" to "I believe this small checker."

I want to be clear about the limits, though. Proving full correctness of a large model like an LLM against some complete specification isn't realistic, partly because we don't even have a formal spec for what "correct" means for language. The guarantees are targeted: specific properties, specific input regions, specific components. And there's a scaling challenge, since formal proofs over huge networks get expensive.

That's also why I'm excited about the connection to AI-assisted theorem proving. Writing these proofs by hand is tedious, but language models are getting quite good at generating Lean proofs, and Lean gives you a perfect verifier, so there's no hallucination problem at the end. Either the proof checks or it doesn't. So the long-term picture is a loop where AI helps write the proofs, and the formal system guarantees they're right. That's how I see us getting from "it seems to work" to "we can actually trust it."

r001.rationale: It defines robustness as limiting output changes when the input is perturbed within a bound.

r002.rationale: It identifies physical constraints, including conservation laws, as properties to certify for scientific machine learning models.

r003.rationale: It identifies floating-point numerical semantics and error bounds as part of the guarantees.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the first thing to be clear about is what kind of guarantee we're even talking about, because people hear "verified neural network" and imagine something like a proof that the model will always classify a stop sign correctly. That's not what we're doing, and honestly I don't think that's a well-posed question for most networks.

What TorchLean does is separate the pieces that are actually provable from the pieces that are empirical. The structure of the network, the shapes, the way operations compose, the arithmetic you're doing in a layer, those are mathematical objects. You can state properties about them and prove them. So we can give you a formal guarantee that the implementation matches the specification, that a gradient computation is actually the gradient of the loss you wrote down, that a Lipschitz bound you're relying on really holds for this architecture, that a certain invariance is exactly preserved and not just approximately preserved. Those are real theorems, checked by Lean, and they don't depend on trusting a test suite.

Then there's the second layer, which is properties on a region of the input space. Robustness around a point, monotonicity in some variable, output staying inside a safe set. Those can be proven too, but the guarantee is conditional on the region you specified. The proof is only as meaningful as the specification. That's actually where most of the hard work is, and it's where I want people to spend their attention. Writing down what you want is harder than proving it.

And then there's everything about the data distribution and what the world will throw at the model, which you cannot prove, and I think it's important to be honest that no verification tool closes that gap. What we can do is make sure that whatever assumptions you're making are explicit, so when something fails you can point to which assumption was violated instead of staring at a black box.

For me the exciting part is less the individual proofs and more that this becomes the interface between the learning and the control or physics side. If I have a neural operator that's a surrogate for a PDE solver, I want to be able to state a conservation law or a stability condition in the same language as the controller that consumes it, and have the whole pipeline checked end to end. That's the kind of guarantee I actually care about for scientific and engineering systems, and that's what we're building toward.

r001.rationale: It mentions robustness around a point and Lipschitz bounds, but does not explain bounding output changes for a specified bound on input perturbation.

r002.rationale: It describes checking a neural operator used as a PDE solver surrogate against conservation laws or stability conditions, which conveys verifying physical-law properties of a neural network solution.

r003.rationale: It mentions proving properties of layer arithmetic, but does not identify bounds on the effects of finite-precision computation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what exactly are you proving, and under what assumptions? You could prove a property of a neural network—for example, that within a specified set of input perturbations, its prediction doesn’t change. That’s a precise, bounded guarantee. It doesn’t establish that the prediction is correct, or that the network will behave reliably on every input it encounters.

For something like TorchLean, I would also want to understand the connection between the mathematical model being verified and the implementation that actually runs. Are you reasoning about exact arithmetic or floating-point computation? Does the guarantee cover the operations used in deployment?

So I see formal verification as a way to make specific claims much more rigorous. The challenge is choosing properties and assumptions that matter in the real world, and then making those proofs scale to useful networks.

r001.rationale: It gives a robustness example: the prediction remains unchanged within a specified set of input perturbations, a zero output change under bounded input perturbation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention physics-informed neural networks or verifying that their solutions satisfy physical laws.

r003.rationale: It raises exact versus floating-point computation and deployment coverage, but does not say TorchLean can bound finite-precision effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between proving that the implementation does what you intended and proving that the network has a particular property. Those are different guarantees. A proof about the code doesn’t automatically establish that the model is robust or that it will generalize.

For a neural network, you could try to establish a precise statement: for every input within a specified region, the output satisfies a particular constraint. If TorchLean produces a proof that Lean checks, then you have a guarantee about that statement, under its assumptions. But those assumptions matter enormously, including how you model numerical computation and what inputs you cover.

For scientific applications, I’m especially interested in properties like conservation laws, symmetries, and stability. Those give us concrete things to formalize. The challenge is connecting that formal guarantee to the physical system. You can prove a property of your mathematical model; whether that model captures the real world still requires scientific validation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions robustness and constraints over an input region, but does not define certified robustness as bounding output perturbations for a specified input perturbation bound.

r002.rationale: It names conservation laws, symmetries, and stability as formalizable scientific properties, but does not identify verifying physics-informed neural network solutions against physical laws as an application.

r003.rationale: It notes that numerical computation affects assumptions, but does not identify bounding finite-precision effects as a guarantee TorchLean can provide.
